div.p: Science is the systematic study of the natural world through observation, experimentation, and reasoning. Scientists ask questions, form hypotheses, collect data, and draw conclusions based on evidence — not opinions or guesses.
The three main branches of science:

ul.li: Life Science — the study of living things (biology)
Physical Science — the study of matter and energy (chemistry + physics)
Earth Science — the study of Earth and space (geology, meteorology, astronomy)

div.p: The scientific method is a step-by-step process scientists use to investigate questions. The steps are not always linear — scientists often loop back and revise.

ol.li: Ask a Question — What do you want to know?
Research — What do you already know? What have others discovered?
Form a Hypothesis — A testable prediction. If… then… because…
Collect Data — Record observations and measurements.
Analyze Data — Look for patterns, calculate averages, make graphs.
Draw Conclusions — Was your hypothesis supported or not?
Communicate Results — Share findings with others.

div.p: Every good experiment has three types of variables:

ul.li: Independent Variable (IV) — The one thing you change on purpose.
Dependent Variable (DV) — The thing you measure; it depends on the IV.
Control Variables (Constants) — Everything that stays the same.

div.p: Control Group: The group that does not receive the experimental treatment. Used for comparison. Example: A plant given no fertilizer while others get fertilizer.
Experimental Group: The group that receives the treatment.

ul.li: Qualitative Data — Descriptions. Uses your senses. ("The liquid turned cloudy.")
Quantitative Data — Numbers. Measurements. ("The liquid reached 45°C.")
Line Graph — Showing change over time.
Pie Chart — Showing parts of a whole.

div.p: Rules for graphing: label both axes with units, give the graph a title like The Effect of [IV] on [DV], use a ruler. Neatness counts.
div.blockquote:
Question: Why does my sandwich bread get soggy when I put sauce on it?
Background research: Bread is porous — it has tiny holes. Sauce has water in it. Water moves from wet things to dry things through a process called diffusion. The bread soaks up the water from the sauce. This is why the bread gets soggy.
Hypothesis: If I put sauce on bread and wait, then the bread will get soggy because the water in the sauce soaks into the bread.
Experiment: Take 3 slices of the same bread. Slice 1 gets no sauce (control). Slice 2 gets 1 tablespoon of sauce. Slice 3 gets 3 tablespoons of sauce. Wait 10 minutes. Measure how soggy each slice is by pressing a paper towel on it and seeing how much water comes off.
Data: Slice 1 — paper towel dry. Slice 2 — small wet spot. Slice 3 — big wet spot, bread falling apart.
Conclusion: The hypothesis was supported. More sauce = more sogginess. The water in the sauce soaks into the bread.
Real-world fix: Put a layer of something between the sauce and the bread — like lettuce, cheese, or butter. Butter is fat and fat blocks water. This is why people butter their bread before making a sandwich.

tr.td: The systematic study of the natural world
A testable prediction based on observations
The variable the scientist changes on purpose
The group that receives no experimental treatment
A factor that stays the same in an experiment
A logical conclusion based on evidence
Information gathered using the five senses
A well-tested explanation supported by much evidence
A rule describing a pattern in nature
A representation used to explain something
